cues.text: A Family Marked for Holiness
Born in 1873 at Alençon, France, Thérèse Martin was the youngest of nine children born to Louis and Zélie Martin.
Both had once hoped to enter religious life themselves before marrying, and five of their surviving children, including Thérèse, would eventually enter religious orders.
Thérèse's mother died of breast cancer when she was only four, a loss that marked her deeply and left her raised largely by her elder sisters.
A Vocation Sought at Fifteen
Determined from childhood to enter the cloistered Carmelite convent at Lisieux, where two of her sisters had already gone, Thérèse was initially refused admission on account of her extreme youth.
Undeterred, she traveled to Rome with her father in 1887 and, during a public audience with Pope Leo XIII, boldly asked him directly to permit her entry.
This unusual act of persistence by an unusually young petitioner, while the pope left the final decision to her local superior, helped secure her admission the following year at fifteen.
The Little Way
Within the ordinary, hidden routine of convent life, Thérèse developed a distinctive spirituality that she called the 'Little Way' .
It was a path to holiness built not on great ascetic feats or visible achievements, but on doing small, ordinary daily acts with total love and complete confidence in God's mercy.
She likened her own soul to a 'little flower' content simply to bloom wherever God had planted it rather than striving to be a more dramatic 'rose.'
Written in Obedience
At her sister and prioress's request, Thérèse spent her final years writing an account of her spiritual life, published after her death as Story of a Soul .
Composed in simple, unpretentious language by a young nun with no formal theological training, the book nonetheless articulated a spirituality of childlike trust.
That spirituality was so compelling that the book quickly became one of the most widely read spiritual autobiographies in the history of the Church.
A Hidden Death
Thérèse contracted tuberculosis and endured a long, physically and spiritually painful final illness, marked at times by profound trials of faith.
By her own account, she bore them in the same spirit of trust that had shaped her whole religious life.
She died at Lisieux in 1897 at only twenty-four, having spent barely nine years within the convent's walls, largely unknown beyond it.
Legacy
The posthumous publication of Story of a Soul transformed Thérèse, within a generation, into one of the most beloved saints in the Catholic world.
She was canonized in 1925 by Pope Pius XI and named co-patroness of the missions despite never having left her cloister.
She was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1997 by Pope John Paul II .
She is one of only four women, and the youngest person, ever to receive that title.
It recognizes a spiritual teaching whose profound simplicity has drawn believers of every background to her 'little way' ever since.
